learning_objective: 🎯 Track exactly where the actual cash came from and where it went, separating normal daily business from investing and financing!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: This is cash generated from the main, core business (like selling shoes if you are a shoe company). We start with Net Profit, but we add back non-cash expenses like Depreciation because they didn't actually reduce our real cash balance.
This is cash spent on or received from long-term assets. Buying a machine is an outflow (-). Selling an old building is an inflow (+). Receiving interest on investments also goes here.
This is cash related to the owners and lenders. Issuing shares or taking a bank loan brings cash IN (+). Paying dividends or paying interest on loans means cash goes OUT (-).

The final result of Operating + Investing + Financing must exactly equal the change in your Cash Equivalents. Equivalents include cash in hand, bank balance, and highly liquid short-term investments (like treasury bills).

fun_activity.title: 🔍 The Wallet Tracker
fun_activity.instructions: Think about your last 3 cash transactions. You bought a sandwich (Operating Outflow). You sold your old bicycle (Investing Inflow). You borrowed ₹500 from your mom (Financing Inflow). Classify your life like a business!

exam_tips: 📌 Depreciation and Amortization (like Goodwill written off) are ALWAYS added back to Net Profit in Operating Activities because no cash actually left the business.
📌 Rule for Working Capital in Operating: Add decrease in Current Assets & increase in Current Liabilities. Subtract increase in Current Assets & decrease in Current Liabilities.
📌 For a Financial Company (like a bank), buying/selling shares or receiving interest is their main job, so it goes in OPERATING. For a normal company, it goes in INVESTING.
quick_recap: ⭐ The Cash Flow Statement is prepared strictly according to Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3).
⭐ It is divided into three buckets: Operating (daily business), Investing (buying/selling assets), and Financing (shares and loans).
⭐ A company can have huge net profits but still have negative cash flow if all sales are on credit!
